theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: You are asked to calibrate a pressure transmitter that is fitted on a working process line. Which document must be in place before you start?

The maker's sales leaflet and price list for a new transmitter

questions.stem: A transmitter marked 'kPa(a)' reads about 101 kPa when its port is open to the air. Why?

questions.stem: What does it mean when a reference gauge's calibration is 'traceable'?

options: Any meter, as long as its battery is new
Any meter, if the job takes only a few minutes

Any meter, if it is kept inside a plastic bag

options: A short or open loop can trip plant or upset control

options: As-found and as-left readings, the reference used and the date

options: A list of the team's lunch orders for the day
A new set of tags for every transmitter
A spare transmitter from the store for each one on the list, just in case

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: You are to calibrate a pressure transmitter fitted on a working pump line. Describe how you would plan and carry out the job safely, from getting the permit to returning the transmitter to service.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first read the data sheet and loop drawing to find the transmitter's range, its tag and the reference I need, and check that the reference gauge or calibrator is in calibration. I would get a permit to work from the person in charge of the plant and agree with the control room operator to put the loop in manual, because the reading will change during the test. I would isolate the transmitter at its block valves, vent and drain the trapped pressure to a safe place and check that it reads zero. If the loop must be disconnected I would isolate its supply as the permit says. I would then connect the hand pump and reference, take as-found readings at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% going up and coming down, adjust zero and span if needed and take as-left readings. Finally I would close the vent, open the valves slowly in the right order, check the live reading with the operator, hand back the permit and complete the calibration record.
markingPoints: Prepares: data sheet, range, reference instrument in calibration
Permit to work and the operator told; loop put in manual
Process isolation: block valves, vent and drain safely, check zero
Five-point check up and down with as-found and as-left readings, adjusting as needed
Returns to service in the right order, checks with the operator, signs off permit and record

essays.stem: Explain how a 4–20 mA signal represents a measurement and why it starts at 4 mA. Then work out the current from a −20 °C to 180 °C temperature transmitter at 130 °C, and the voltage this gives across a 250 Ω resistor. Show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: A 4–20 mA signal sends the measurement as a current. 4 mA is the bottom of the range (0%) and 20 mA is the top (100%), so the 16 mA in between is the span. A current is used because it does not change with the length or resistance of the cable. Starting at 4 mA, a 'live zero', means a two-wire transmitter still gets power at the bottom of its range, and a reading near 0 mA can only mean a fault such as a broken wire. For the transmitter: the span is 180 − (−20) = 200 °C. The measured value above the bottom is 130 − (−20) = 150 °C. 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, or 75% of span. Current = 4 + (0.75 × 16) = 4 + 12 = 16 mA. Voltage across 250 Ω = 0.016 A × 250 Ω = 4 V.
markingPoints: 4 mA = 0% and 20 mA = 100%; current is not affected by cable resistance
Live zero: powers the transmitter and shows a broken loop as a fault
Span 200 °C and 75% of span worked out
Current = 16 mA, with working shown
Voltage = 4 V across 250 Ω

essays.stem: Compare a thermocouple and an RTD (such as a Pt100). Say which you would choose for a hot-water line at about 80 °C and which for a furnace flue at about 700 °C, and explain why.
essays.modelAnswer: A thermocouple is two different metals joined at the tip. Heating the tip makes a small voltage that the instrument reads, after allowing for the temperature at its own end (cold junction compensation). Thermocouples are tough, respond quickly and work to very high temperatures, but they are less accurate and must be extended with the matching compensating or extension cable. An RTD such as a Pt100 is a platinum element whose resistance rises with temperature: 100 Ω at 0 °C and about 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. It is more accurate and stable, and a three-wire or four-wire connection cancels the lead resistance, but it is more fragile and is mainly used at lower temperatures. For the hot-water line at 80 °C I would choose a Pt100 in a thermowell, because accuracy matters and the temperature is low. For the furnace flue at 700 °C I would choose a suitable thermocouple, such as type K, because it can stand the heat.
markingPoints: Thermocouple: two metals make a voltage; needs cold junction compensation and matching cable
RTD: resistance rises with temperature; Pt100 = 100 Ω at 0 °C
RTD more accurate; 3- or 4-wire connection cancels lead resistance
Chooses the RTD for 80 °C with a reason
Chooses a thermocouple for 700 °C with a reason

essays.stem: Explain how a pressure transmitter at the bottom of a tank can be used to measure level. Work out the pressure at the bottom of an open tank holding 4 m of water, and explain what would happen to the reading if the tank were filled with a lighter liquid.
essays.modelAnswer: The weight of liquid above a point makes a pressure that rises with depth. A pressure transmitter fitted at the bottom of an open tank therefore reads a pressure that is proportional to the height of liquid above it, and it can be ranged so that 4 mA is empty and 20 mA is full. For water, each metre of depth gives about 9.81 kPa. For 4 m of water: 4 × 9.81 = 39.24 kPa, so about 39 kPa. The pressure also depends on the density of the liquid. A lighter liquid such as oil gives less pressure for the same depth, so a transmitter set up for water would read lower than the true level. The range must be worked out for the actual liquid, and the tank must be vented, or a differential pressure transmitter must be used to take away the gas pressure above the liquid in a closed tank.
markingPoints: Pressure rises with depth, so pressure shows the height of liquid
About 9.81 kPa per metre of water
4 m gives about 39 kPa, with working
A lighter liquid gives less pressure, so the level reads low
Range set for the real liquid; DP transmitter for closed tanks

essays.stem: Explain what traceable calibration means, why the reference instrument must be more accurate than the one being checked, and what must be done when an instrument is found to be out of tolerance.
essays.modelAnswer: Traceable calibration means the reference used to check an instrument has itself been checked against a more accurate standard, and that one against another, in an unbroken chain back to national measurement standards. Each step has a certificate with a date and the results, so anyone can show the reading is right. The reference should be several times more accurate than the instrument under test (a ratio of about four to one is often used), so that its own small error does not decide whether the instrument passes or fails. When an instrument is found out of tolerance, the as-found readings are recorded before any adjustment. It is then adjusted and the as-left readings recorded, or it is tagged out of use if it cannot be adjusted. The fault is reported to the supervisor, because every reading taken since the last good check may be wrong, and work or product that relied on it may need to be reviewed. The calibration interval may need to be shortened.
markingPoints: Traceable: unbroken chain of certified checks back to national standards
Reference several times more accurate so its error does not decide the result
As-found readings recorded before adjusting; as-left after
Tags out of use if it cannot be corrected
Reports it so earlier readings and work can be reviewed; interval reviewed

essays.stem: A level reading in the control room shows below 4 mA (a 'low fault'). Describe how you would find the fault, safely, using a loop drawing and a loop calibrator.
essays.modelAnswer: A reading below 4 mA means the loop is not working, because a healthy transmitter never sends less than 4 mA. First I would get the permit and tell the operator, so the reading can be ignored and the loop put in manual. I would read the loop drawing to find the power supply, the fuse or barrier, the junction box terminals and the panel input. With the operator's agreement I would measure the loop supply voltage at the panel, which is usually 24 V DC. If there is no supply, I check the fuse and the power supply unit. If the supply is there, I would check the loop current at the junction box and at the transmitter, to find where it is lost. I would isolate the loop and check the cable for a broken or loose wire with a continuity test. If the cable is good, I would use the loop calibrator to send 4, 12 and 20 mA into the panel input to prove the panel, then check the transmitter itself. I would repair the fault, test the loop and record what I found.
markingPoints: Knows below 4 mA means a fault, not a low process value
Permit and operator told; loop in manual
Uses the loop drawing to follow supply, fuse, junction box and input
Logical checks: supply, current along the loop, continuity with the loop isolated
Uses the loop calibrator to prove the panel input; repairs, tests and records

essays.stem: Describe the main hazards when working on instruments connected to a process line, and how a lead technician would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Stored pressure is the first hazard: a fitting opened under pressure can blow out with force. It is controlled by isolating at the block valves, venting and draining to a safe place and proving zero before any fitting is loosened. Hot fluids such as steam or hot water can scald, so the line is allowed to cool and gloves and a face shield are worn. Chemicals such as caustic soda or acids need chemical gloves, eye and face protection and flushing of the impulse lines, as the permit and the safety data sheet say. Electrical supplies to transmitters and panels are isolated, locked and tagged and proved dead where the permit requires it. In an area shown as hazardous on the area classification drawing, only certified equipment is used, under a permit, by authorised people. The process itself is a hazard, since a wrong signal can trip or upset the plant, so the operator puts the loop in manual. The lead technician briefs the team on all of this before work starts.
markingPoints: Stored pressure: isolate, vent, drain, prove zero
Heat and chemicals: cool down, correct PPE, flush lines, follow the SDS
Electrical isolation, lock and tag where needed
Hazardous areas: certified equipment, permit, authorised people only
Process upset: operator told, loop in manual; team briefed

essays.stem: You lead a team of three on a plant shutdown. Explain how you would make sure the instrument readings and calibration records they produce are accurate and complete.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the work, I would give each person a list of the instruments they are to check, with the tag, range, test points and acceptance tolerance, and a standard record sheet. I would check that every reference instrument has an in-date calibration label and show the team how to read it. I would brief them on the method: as-found readings first, five points up and down, the correct units, and no adjustment until the as-found readings are written down. During the work I would watch each person do at least one check, and look at their sheets as they go, so mistakes are caught early. If a reading looked wrong, such as a level over 100%, I would ask how it was taken and have it repeated, rather than change it myself. At the end I would check that every sheet is complete, signed and dated, that any failures are tagged and reported, and that the records are filed where the plant keeps them.
markingPoints: Gives each member a clear task list with ranges, tolerances and a standard sheet
Checks reference instruments are in calibration
Briefs the method: as-found first, five points, units
Supervises and checks records during the work; repeats doubtful readings
Final check: complete, signed sheets, failures tagged and reported, records filed

essays.stem: Explain why the flow through an orifice plate is not in a straight line with the differential pressure. A transmitter shows 64% of its maximum differential pressure: work out the percentage of maximum flow, and say how the control system usually deals with this.
essays.modelAnswer: An orifice plate makes the fluid speed up through a smaller hole, and the pressure drops. The pressure drop rises with the square of the flow, so doubling the flow gives four times the differential pressure. This means the flow is found from the square root of the differential pressure, not from the differential pressure itself. At 64% of maximum differential pressure, the flow is the square root of 0.64, which is 0.8, so the flow is 80% of maximum. Without correction, a reading of 64% would be badly wrong. The control system or the transmitter usually applies a square-root function, so the signal it shows is in step with the flow. The square-root function is set in either the transmitter or the panel, not both, otherwise the reading will be wrong again. Readings at very low flow are less reliable, so many systems cut off the display near zero flow.
markingPoints: Differential pressure rises with the square of flow
Flow is found from the square root of the differential pressure
Square root of 0.64 = 0.8, so flow is 80%
Square-root function set in the transmitter or the panel, not both
Notes poor accuracy at very low flow

essays.stem: Describe what a calibration report or certificate for a field transmitter should contain, and explain why each part is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should give the transmitter's tag number, maker, model and serial number, so there is no doubt which instrument was checked. It should give its range and the tolerance it must meet, so the results can be judged. It should list the reference instruments used, with their serial numbers and calibration due dates, to show the check is traceable. It should give the as-found readings at each test point, up and down, and the error at each point, followed by any adjustment made and the as-left readings, so anyone can see how far it had drifted. It should state clearly whether the transmitter passed or failed, with the date, the name and signature of the technician and the date of the next check. Any problems found, such as a blocked impulse line, and any follow-up needed should be noted. These records are used to plan maintenance, to set calibration intervals, and to prove the plant's measurements are correct during an audit.
markingPoints: Identifies the instrument: tag, model, serial number, range and tolerance
References used, with serial numbers and calibration dates
As-found readings, errors, adjustments and as-left readings
Pass or fail, date, name, signature and next due date
Notes problems and follow-up; explains uses for maintenance and audit

practical1.title: Five-point calibration of a pressure transmitter on a training bench
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and carry out a five-point calibration of a 4–20 mA pressure transmitter mounted on the Centre's instrument training bench, and issue a calibration record. One member is the lead and writes a short job plan (tag, range, tolerance, references, steps, hazards). Two members connect the hand pump, reference gauge and loop with the 24 V DC bench supply switched off; the assessor checks the wiring and switches the supply on. Members then take turns to apply pressure, read the reference and read the mA output, taking as-found readings at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% going up and coming down. The group works out the error at each point as a percentage of span, decides whether the transmitter passes, makes any zero and span adjustment the assessor allows, takes as-left readings and completes the record. Every member makes at least two readings and signs the record for the part they did. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Instrument training bench with a 4–20 mA pressure transmitter (0–600 kPa or similar)
Hand pressure pump, hoses and fittings
Reference pressure gauge or calibrator with an in-date calibration label
24 V DC loop power supply (switched by the assessor)
Multimeter or loop calibrator for reading mA
Job plan form and calibration record sheet
photos: The written job plan, with the transmitter's range, tolerance and the references listed
The loop and pump connections made with the supply off, before the assessor's check
A reading being taken: reference gauge and mA reading both visible
The completed as-found table with errors worked out
The as-left readings after any adjustment
The signed calibration record and the bench left tidy, supply off
checklist: Took part in writing the job plan, including range, tolerance and hazards
Checked the reference instrument's calibration label before use
Made connection changes only with the supply switched off
Applied pressure steadily and did not exceed the transmitter's range
Read the reference and the mA output correctly, with units
Worked out the error as a percentage of span correctly
Recorded as-found readings before any adjustment
Signed the record for their own readings and left the bench safe
safety: Only the assessor switches the 24 V DC supply on; all wiring changes are made with it off
Never apply more pressure than the transmitter or hoses are rated for; release pressure before disconnecting
Wear safety glasses while the pump and hoses are under pressure
Keep hoses tidy and the floor clear to prevent trips

practical2.title: Temperature loop check with an RTD and a thermocouple
practical2.brief: As a group, check two temperature measurement loops on the Centre's training board: one with a Pt100 RTD and one with a type K thermocouple, each wired to a temperature transmitter or indicator. The board is dead while you work. First, two members inspect the wiring against the loop drawing and correct any fault the assessor has planted (for example a two-wire RTD connection where three are needed, or a copper extension on the thermocouple). The assessor then switches the board on. Next, members place each sensor beside a reference thermometer in a dry-block calibrator (or a container of warm water below 60 °C and a container of iced water) and record the reading at three temperatures. The group also uses a loop calibrator to check the indicator at 4, 12 and 20 mA. Finally, the lead writes a short loop check report that states what was found, what was corrected and whether each loop passes. Each member leads at least one part and signs for it. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Training board with a Pt100 RTD loop and a type K thermocouple loop (transmitters or indicators)
Dry-block calibrator, or insulated containers of iced water and warm water
Reference thermometer with an in-date calibration label
Type K compensating cable, small screwdrivers and ferrules
Loop check sheet and report form
photos: Both loops inspected against the drawing, with the planted fault marked
The fault corrected, with the board still dead
Each sensor beside the reference thermometer at one test temperature
The loop calibrator connected to the indicator input
The completed loop check sheet with three temperature points for each loop
The signed loop check report and the work area cleared
checklist: Checked the wiring against the loop drawing with the board dead
Found and correctly fixed the planted fault (3-wire RTD or correct compensating cable)
Placed the sensor and reference together and waited for the readings to settle
Recorded readings at three temperatures for each loop with correct units
